t.1.56.1: Janamejaya said: You have indeed told it all in brief, O best of the twice-born: the Mahābhārata, the tale, the great history of the Kurus.
t.1.56.3: Therefore, sir, you should tell this story again in full detail, for I am never sated as I listen to the great deeds of my forefathers.
t.1.56.2: As you, O sinless one, relate this tale of wondrous import, an exceedingly great curiosity has arisen in me to hear it in full detail.
t.1.56.4: For that cause was no small one, in which the Pāṇḍavas, knowers of dharma, slew in every way those who should not be slain, and yet they are praised by men.
t.1.56.5: Why did those tigers among men, though they were capable and indeed blameless, patiently endure the torments inflicted upon them by the wicked?
t.1.56.6: How did Vṛkodara, mighty of arm and possessing the strength of ten thousand elephants, restrain his anger even while being sorely harassed, O best of the twice-born?
t.1.56.7: How is it that Draupadī Kṛṣṇā, that virtuous woman, though she was able, did not burn the Dhārtarāṣṭras with her terrible gaze while she was being tormented by those evil-hearted men?
t.1.56.9: How did Yudhiṣṭhira, the best of those who uphold dharma, the son of Dharma and knower of dharma, endure such supreme hardship, undeserving of it as he was?
t.1.56.8: How was it that, at the dicing, he passed over the two Pārthas and likewise the two sons of Mādrī, and followed that tiger among men as he was being deceived by the evil-minded ones?
t.1.56.10: And how did Dhanaṃjaya, the Pāṇḍava with Kṛṣṇa as his charioteer, alone, shooting his arrows, send all those numerous armies to the world of the ancestors?
t.1.56.11: Tell me all this exactly as it happened, O ascetic rich in austerities, and whatever those great chariot-warriors did here and there.
t.1.56.12: I shall declare in full the thought of the great seer Vyāsa, the great-souled one of boundless splendour, who is revered in all the worlds.
t.1.56.13: For this collection of a hundred thousand verses about those of meritorious deeds has been expounded here by the son of Satyavatī, of immeasurable energy.
t.1.56.14: The learned man who recites this, and the man who listens to it, both reach the abode of Brahmā and attain equality with the gods.
t.1.56.16: In this most holy history, artha and dharma are taught in their entirety, and so too is the ultimate understanding.
t.1.56.15: For this is equal to the Vedas, holy and supreme; and this ancient lore, praised by the seers, is the best of all things worth hearing.
t.1.56.18: Having heard this history, even a man of exceedingly cruel nature would without doubt cast off the sin committed through the killing of an embryo.
t.1.56.17: The learned man who makes those who are not base, who are given to generosity, devoted to truth, and not unbelievers, listen to this Veda of Kṛṣṇa obtains his aim.
t.1.56.19: This history, called Jaya, should be heard by one who desires victory; he conquers the whole earth and would also vanquish his enemies.
t.1.56.20: This is the best means of obtaining a son, this is a great bringer of well-being; it should likewise be heard many times by the chief queen and the crown prince.
t.1.56.21: This is a holy treatise on worldly profit, this is the supreme treatise on dharma, and this is a treatise on liberation, proclaimed by Vyāsa of boundless wisdom.
t.1.56.23: Whatever sin has been committed by body, by speech, and by mind, all of it a man quickly casts off when he constantly listens to this.
t.1.56.22: Some recount it even now, and others likewise will recount it in the future. For such a person, sons are obedient and servants do what is pleasing.
t.1.56.24: For those who listen without envy to the great birth of the Bhāratas, there is no fear of disease; how then could there be fear of the world beyond?
t.1.56.25: This work, which brings wealth, fame, long life, heaven, and merit as well, was composed by Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, who desired to bring about merit.
t.1.56.26: By him who spread throughout the world the fame of the great-souled Pāṇḍavas and of the other kṣatriyas, rich in wealth and splendour.
t.1.56.27: Just as the blessed ocean and just as Himavat, the mountain, are both renowned as treasuries of jewels, so too is the Bhārata said to be.
t.1.56.28: The learned man who recites this to brāhmaṇas here on the days of the moon's changes, his sins shaken off and heaven won, attains oneness with brahman.
t.1.56.29: Whoever recites this to the brāhmaṇas at a śrāddha, even if only a single quarter-verse, makes that śrāddha of his imperishable, and it reaches the ancestors as well.
t.1.56.31: The great birth of the Bhāratas is called the Mahābhārata. He who knows this explanation of its name is released from all sins.
t.1.56.30: Whatever sin a man commits through ignorance in the course of a day as he goes about, that is dissolved merely by hearing the tale of the Mahābhārata.
t.1.56.32: In three years, constantly rising early to his work, the sage Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana composed this supreme narrative, the Mahābhārata.
t.1.56.33: O bull among the Bharatas, in matters of law, wealth, pleasure, and liberation, whatever is found here may be found elsewhere, but what is not found here is found nowhere.
